items.readable_text:
Content:
When writing out a sum, we often have to write a lot of terms. For example, the following sum has five terms:

Content:
[MATH: S = 2+4+6+8+10]

Content:
We could just as easily encounter a sum with ten terms, or a hundred terms, or a thousand terms, or even more!

Content:
Thankfully, there is a notation called sigma notation that allows us to write sums more compactly, without writing every term.

Content:
To express the given sum [MATH: S] using sigma notation, we first need to come up with the general term [MATH: a_n] in our sum. Here, the [MATH: n]th term of our sum has the form [MATH: a_n = 2n,] where [MATH: n] ranges from [MATH: {\color{red}1}] to [MATH: {\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: a_{1}|= 2(1) = 2; a_{2}|= 2(2) = 4; a_{3}|= 2(3) = 6; a_{4}|= 2(4) = 8; a_{5}|= 2(5) = 10]

Content:
So, our sum can be written as
[MATH: S = a_{\color{red}1} + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 + a_{\color{blue}5}.]

Content:
Finally, we use the Greek letter [MATH: \displaystyle\sum] (called "sigma") to denote our summation:
[MATH: S = ∑_(n = 1)^(5)(a_{n}) = ∑_(n = 1)^(5)(2n)]

Content:
We write the [MATH: n]th term [MATH: ({\color{black}a_n=2n})] to the right of [MATH: \displaystyle\sum,] we put the first index [MATH: ({\color{red}1})] below the sigma as [MATH: n={\color{red}1},] and we put the last index [MATH: ({\color{blue}5})] above the sigma.

Content:
We can retrieve the expanded sum by substituting all values between [MATH: \color{red}1] and [MATH: \color{blue}5] into the [MATH: n]th term, and separating each result with a "[MATH: +]" sign, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(5)(2n)|= 2(1) + 2(2) + 2(3) + 2(4) + 2(5); = 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10]

Content:
Note: The sum

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{5} 2n = 2+4+6+8+10]

Content:
is an example of a series. A series is what we get when we add the terms of a sequence together. In this case, we're summing the terms of the sequence [MATH: a_n = 2n.]

sections.normalized_html: Express [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{4} (2n-3)] as a sum of three terms.
sections.readable_text: Express [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{4} (2n-3)] as a sum of three terms.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The sum takes integer values of [MATH: n] from [MATH: 2] to [MATH: 4.] So, we compute the terms for [MATH: n=2,3,4] and write the sum, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{4}(2n-3)&= \overbrace{\big(2(2)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,2}+\overbrace{\big(2(3)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,3}+\overbrace{\big(2(4)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,4} \[-5pt] &=(4-3)+(6-3)+(8-3)\[5pt] &=1+3+5 }]

&=(4-3)+(6-3)+(8-3)\[5pt]
&=1+3+5
}]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Express [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{4} (2n-3)] as a sum of three terms.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The sum takes integer values of [MATH: n] from [MATH: 2] to [MATH: 4.] So, we compute the terms for [MATH: n=2,3,4] and write the sum, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{4}(2n-3)&= \overbrace{\big(2(2)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,2}+\overbrace{\big(2(3)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,3}+\overbrace{\big(2(4)-3\big)}^{\large n\,=\,4} \[-5pt]
&=(4-3)+(6-3)+(8-3)\[5pt]
&=1+3+5
}]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to express the following series in sigma notation.

Content:
[MATH: S = \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2} + \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3} + \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4} + \cdots + \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20} + \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
To do this, we first examine the numerators and denominators of the corresponding sequence.

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
Our goal is to find a pattern in the terms. To do this, we note the following:

Content:
- The numerators form the following sequence:
[MATH: {\color{red}1}, \quad {\color{red}2}, \quad {\color{red}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{red}19}, \quad {\color{red}20}]
Notice that we have [MATH: 20] terms in total. The [MATH: n]th term of this sequence is given by
[MATH: {\color{red}a_n} = {\color{red}n}, \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.]
- The denominators form the following sequence:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2}, \quad {\color{blue}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{blue}20}, \quad {\color{blue}21}]
Since the value in the denominator is always one more than the numerator, the [MATH: n]th term of this sequence is given by
[MATH: {\color{blue}b_n} = {\color{blue}n + 1} , \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.]

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
is

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}a_n}{\color{blue}b_n} =\dfrac{\color{red}n}{\color{blue}n+1},]
where [MATH: n] ranges from [MATH: n=1] to [MATH: n=20.]

Content:
Therefore, we can express our series using sigma notation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: S = ∑_(n = 1)^(20)(n)/(n + 1).]

Content:
We can check that this answer is correct by writing out the summation in full and checking that we recover the original sequence:

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(20)(n)/(n + 1)|= (1)/(1 + 1) + (2)/(2 + 1) + ⋯ + (19)/(19 + 1) + (20)/(20 + 1); = (1)/(2) + (2)/(3) + ⋯ + (19)/(20) + (20)/(21)✓]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the terms of the corresponding sequence

[MATH: 4, \quad 8, \quad 12, \quad , \ldots, \quad 56, \quad 60.] are multiples of [MATH: 4,] and since [MATH: 60\div 4 = 15,] there are [MATH: 15] terms in total.

Therefore, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence has the form [MATH: a_n =4n,] where [MATH: n] ranges from [MATH: n=1] to [MATH: n=15\mathbin{.}] Indeed:

[MATH: a_{1}|= 4(1) = 4; a_{2}|= 4(2) = 8; a_{3}|= 4(3) = 12; ⋮; a_{14}|= 4(14) = 56; a_{15}|= 4(15) = 60]

Therefore,

[MATH: \eqalign{ S=4+8+12+\cdots+56+60=\sum_{n=1}^{15} 4n. }]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Expressing Sums in Sigma Notation

Content:
Suppose we want to express the following series in sigma notation.

Content:
[MATH: S = \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2} + \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3} + \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4} + \cdots + \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20} + \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
To do this, we first examine the numerators and denominators of the corresponding sequence.

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
Our goal is to find a pattern in the terms. To do this, we note the following:

Content:
- The numerators form the following sequence:
[MATH: {\color{red}1}, \quad {\color{red}2}, \quad {\color{red}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{red}19}, \quad {\color{red}20}]
Notice that we have [MATH: 20] terms in total. The [MATH: n]th term of this sequence is given by
[MATH: {\color{red}a_n} = {\color{red}n}, \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.]
- The denominators form the following sequence:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2}, \quad {\color{blue}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{blue}20}, \quad {\color{blue}21}]
Since the value in the denominator is always one more than the numerator, the [MATH: n]th term of this sequence is given by
[MATH: {\color{blue}b_n} = {\color{blue}n + 1} , \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.]

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}]

Content:
is

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}a_n}{\color{blue}b_n} =\dfrac{\color{red}n}{\color{blue}n+1},]
where [MATH: n] ranges from [MATH: n=1] to [MATH: n=20.]

Content:
Therefore, we can express our series using sigma notation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: S = ∑_(n = 1)^(20)(n)/(n + 1).]

Content:
We can check that this answer is correct by writing out the summation in full and checking that we recover the original sequence:

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(20)(n)/(n + 1)|= (1)/(1 + 1) + (2)/(2 + 1) + ⋯ + (19)/(19 + 1) + (20)/(20 + 1); = (1)/(2) + (2)/(3) + ⋯ + (19)/(20) + (20)/(21)✓]

Item 9 — Example: Writing Sums Using Sigma Notation

Example Prompt:
Express [MATH: S=4+8+12+\cdots+56+60] in sigma notation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that the terms of the corresponding sequence

[MATH: 4, \quad 8, \quad 12, \quad , \ldots, \quad 56, \quad 60.]
are multiples of [MATH: 4,] and since [MATH: 60\div 4 = 15,] there are [MATH: 15] terms in total.

Therefore, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence has the form
[MATH: a_n =4n,]
where [MATH: n] ranges from [MATH: n=1] to [MATH: n=15\mathbin{.}] Indeed:

[MATH: a_{1}|= 4(1) = 4; a_{2}|= 4(2) = 8; a_{3}|= 4(3) = 12; ⋮; a_{14}|= 4(14) = 56; a_{15}|= 4(15) = 60]

Therefore,

[MATH: \eqalign{
S=4+8+12+\cdots+56+60=\sum_{n=1}^{15} 4n.
}]
